strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem diagnosis: the paper convincingly articulates three concrete pitfalls (approximate layer-wise solutions, model-wide suboptimality, surrogate-objective mismatch) of the dominant layer-wise reconstruction paradigm, and the 'surrogate-free' reformulation is a sensible and principled response.

Strong and consistent empirical gains precisely where prior methods fail: at 70-90% sparsity ELSA dramatically outperforms seven baselines across six models (e.g., 23.14 vs ~181 C4 perplexity on LLaMA-2-7B at 90%), and establishes a new Pareto frontier in perplexity vs. non-zero parameters (Figure 3).

Broad evaluation coverage: perplexity on two datasets, seven zero-shot tasks, N:M semi-structured patterns, non-uniform sparsity allocation (OWL/EvoPress comparisons), and scaling to 27B with a low-precision variant; ablations isolate the contribution of the NTP objective and the Fisher-based projection.

The paper includes a convergence analysis for both the standard and quantized-state variants, which is unusual rigor for this sub-field, and addresses a practical scalability concern (FP8/INT8 ADMM states, FSDP-2) rather than stopping at small-scale demos.
Honest discussion section that re-examines the memory-efficiency assumptions of layer-wise methods and acknowledges limitations.
weaknesses: Compute cost is not reported or compared. ELSA performs 4,096 optimization steps at batch size 8 with full training machinery, whereas baselines like Wanda/SparseGPT are one-shot (minutes on a single GPU). Without wall-clock/GPU-hour comparisons, the headline results conflate algorithmic improvement with a much larger compute budget; this is the most significant fairness concern.

Data budget is not controlled. ELSA uses 'larger calibration sets' than the baselines, and the paper's own ablation (Figure 6) shows NTP-based pruning keeps improving with more data while REM saturates. It is unclear how much of the gain comes from the formulation versus simply more data and optimization steps. A compute/data-matched comparison is missing.

ELSA underperforms at moderate sparsity (50-60%): e.g., on LLaMA-2-7B at 50% it trails L-ADMM/ALPS noticeably (53.35 vs 57.73 avg accuracy), and at 90% perplexity (26.97) is still ~5x the dense model (5.47). The abstract's 'high model fidelity' and 'up to 90% without significant performance degradation' framing is stronger than the evidence.

Per-cell hyperparameter tuning (Table 5 lists distinct learning rates and penalty schedules for every model-sparsity combination) raises overfitting-to-evaluation concerns; it is unclear how systematically baselines were tuned in comparison.

Theory-practice gap: the convergence analysis assumes exact Hessian-based subproblems and (λ−μ)-strong convexity conditions, while the practical method uses a Diag(Fisher) approximation (via Adam moments) and cosine penalty schedules not covered by the theory; λ-stationarity is also a fairly weak guarantee, and weak convexity of the NTP loss is a strong assumption for transformers.

Component novelty is moderate: ADMM for ℓ0-constrained network training is well established (L-ADMM and earlier work), and Fisher/Diag-Hessian importance weighting for pruning follows Optimal Brain Damage/Surgeon lineage and recent 'Fisher-for-free' work; the contribution is mainly the global surrogate-free formulation applied to LLMs rather than new algorithmic primitives.

Some baselines are incompletely evaluated (SparseLLM missing on several models), and a few details (e.g., the constant α in the appendix, exact calibration set sizes for ELSA vs. baselines) are under-specified, partially hurting reproducibility despite the promised code release.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and well-motivated question: whether the 'sparsity wall' at ~50-70% for LLM pruning is an inherent limitation or an artifact of the prevailing layer-wise reconstruction-error formulation.

The empirical sweep is broad: 6 model families/scales (OPT-125M to Gemma-2-27B), sparsity levels from 50% to 90%, structured (N:M) and non-uniform sparsity patterns, plus perplexity and zero-shot evaluation across 7 tasks.

Results at extreme sparsity (80-90%) are genuinely striking relative to prior one-shot methods (e.g., LLaMA-2-7B at 90%: 26.97 vs. 248.8 for the best baseline on WikiText), and Figure 3's Pareto analysis is a nice way to summarize the contribution.

The inclusion of a convergence analysis (for both the exact and quantized-state variants) and a memory-efficient ELSA-L variant that scales to 27B with fp8 ADMM states adds technical depth beyond a purely empirical contribution.
Ablations on the objective (NTP vs. reconstruction error) and the Fisher-based projection step are sensible and support the design choices.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded by a large compute and data asymmetry. Baselines (Wanda, SparseGPT, ALPS, etc.) are essentially one-shot/training-free methods using 128 calibration sequences, while ELSA performs 4,096 optimization steps of full-model training with Adam on 'larger calibration sets' (size unspecified in the main text). The paper does not report wall-clock time, GPU-hours, or FLOPs for any method. Without a fine-tuning-based control (e.g., pruning with SparseGPT followed by LoRA/full recovery training at the same budget), it is impossible to tell how much of the gain comes from the 'surrogate-free' formulation versus simply training much longer.

Performance at moderate sparsity — where baselines are practical — is actually worse for ELSA: on LLaMA-2-7B at 50%, ELSA's perplexity (8.08) trails SAFE (6.72) and L-ADMM (6.80), and its zero-shot average (53.35) trails all learning-based baselines (up to 57.73). Similar inversions appear on LLaMA-2-13B and in the N:M results (Table 1). The practical envelope of the method is therefore quite narrow, which the framing understates.

The claim of 'retaining high model fidelity' / 'without significant performance degradation' at 90% sparsity is overstated: perplexity of 26.97 vs. dense 5.47 on LLaMA-2-7B, and zero-shot averages of 38.52 vs. 59.67 dense, with some tasks (e.g., ARC-C at 18.52) near or below the random-chance baselines of weaker methods. The improvement over baselines is real but the absolute quality is severely degraded.

A gap between theory and practice: the convergence analysis assumes exact (or γ-accurate) minimization of the x-subproblem and the Euclidean/Fisher projection, whereas the implementation uses Adam updates, Diag(F) weighting, cosine-scheduled penalties, and fp8-quantized states with dynamically updated scales; whether Theorem 4.6's conditions hold under these approximations is not discussed. Also, the 27B result is a single model at a single sparsity level, limiting the scalability evidence.

Heavy per-configuration hyperparameter tuning (Table 5 shows distinct learning rates and penalty schedules for each model/sparsity combination) raises concerns about evaluation overfitting and reproducibility; baselines appear to be run with default settings, potentially disadvantaging them.

Baselines are somewhat under-served: SparseLLM could not be run on 3 of 6 models, and recent related global/non-uniform pruning approaches are given limited treatment. The EvoPress comparison (Table 2) uses hyperparameters from a different model (LLaMA-2-7B) for LLaMA-3-8B.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'researchers has begun', 'vayring', 'constrat', 'a experiment'), Figure 4's radar plots are hard to read, and the effective calibration-set size for ELSA is not clearly stated anywhere in the main text despite being central to fairness of comparison.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper convincingly argues that the layer-wise reconstruction surrogate (eq. 2-3) is the root cause of the 'sparsity wall' at 50-60%, and directly targets the true constrained objective (eq. 1) via ADMM.

Substantial and consistent empirical gains in the extreme-sparsity regime (70-90%) across six models spanning 125M to 27B and four architectures, with both perplexity (Table 6) and zero-shot accuracy (Tables 7-8); the reported 7.8x perplexity improvement at 90% on LLaMA-2-7B is well supported by the detailed tables in the appendix.

A genuinely useful scalability contribution: ELSA-L with quantized auxiliary states (bf16/fp8) enables 27B pruning with 66% memory reduction, and the paper provides a non-trivial convergence proof for the quantized variant (Theorem 4.6), which is rarely done for such low-precision modifications.

Good experimental breadth beyond unstructured sparsity: N:M semi-structured patterns, non-uniform sparsity allocations (OWL/EvoPress comparisons), and ablations (NTP vs. REM data scaling, objective-aware projection) that directly support the paper's central argument.

The discussion in Section 6 (e.g., the counterintuitive point that layer-wise methods may be less memory-efficient than assumed due to calibration activation storage) is thoughtful and adds value beyond the method itself.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness regarding compute budget: ELSA trains for 4,096 steps with a large calibration set, whereas SparseGPT/Wanda and similar baselines are one-shot methods using 128 calibration sequences. The paper does not report wall-clock time, GPU-hours, or data/compute-matched comparisons, so a large part of the gains may simply reflect a much larger pruning budget rather than the surrogate-free formulation per se. The NTP-vs-REM ablation (Fig. 6) actually highlights this data dependence but does not control for it.

ELSA underperforms strong baselines at moderate sparsity (50-60%): e.g., at 50% on LLaMA-2-7B, ELSA averages 53.35% vs. 57.73% (L-ADMM) and 57.14% (ALPS), and it is behind on many entries in Table 6 at 50%. The paper's positioning is entirely around extreme sparsity, but the practical value at 50-70% (where the described 'sparsity wall' mostly does not bind) is weak, and this trade-off is not clearly acknowledged.

The convergence analysis is largely standard ADMM theory adapted to the setting; it relies on strong assumptions for neural network objectives (weak convexity, bounded iterates, exact inexactness parameters), and the λ-stationarity notion is weak. The main practical algorithm (objective-aware projection, Diag(Fisher), Adam-based x-update) is not fully covered by the theory.

Hyperparameter configuration appears fragile: learning rates as large as 2e-1 and varying penalty schedules across models/sparsities (Table 5) suggest significant per-configuration tuning; no sensitivity analysis is provided, which weakens reproducibility claims.

Several writing issues and minor inconsistencies: grammatical errors ('researchers has begun', 'vayring', 'constrat'), a missing URL for the promised source code, incomplete sentences, and an inconsistent 7.8x claim relative to which baseline/dataset it refers to.
RTE accuracy appears saturated at ~52.71-54.79 for all methods at high sparsity, suggesting possible evaluation degeneracy on that task, which inflates the apparent margins.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper convincingly identifies concrete limitations of layer-wise reconstruction-error minimization (error compounding, sequential suboptimality, surrogate-objective mismatch) and proposes a principled direct formulation (1) of pruning as sparsity-constrained optimization on the true NTP objective.

Strong and extensive empirical evidence: the method is evaluated across four model families (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2/3) spanning 125M to 27B, at sparsity levels from 50% to 99%, with comprehensive baselines (Magnitude, SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS, L-ADMM, SAFE, SparseLLM). The order-of-magnitude perplexity improvements at 80-90%+ sparsity are large and consistent across models (Table 10).

Practical relevance is well established: the paper does not stop at perplexity, but reports end-to-end latency/throughput/memory with a real SpMV kernel (Table 1), a cost-quality analysis in GPU-hours against matched-budget retraining baselines (Table 3), zero-shot task accuracy (Table 11/12), and scaling to 27B with FP8 states (Figure 5).
Includes non-trivial theoretical contribution: a convergence guarantee for the quantized ADMM variant (Theorem 4.6 / Appendix A), which is the practically used algorithm, with a complete proof.

Good ablations: NTP vs. REM objective (data efficiency of the surrogate-free objective), Fisher-aware projection (Table 9), extensions to N:M and non-uniform sparsity (Tables 7-8), and a thoughtful discussion of the memory-efficiency assumptions underlying layer-wise methods.
Reproducibility effort appears solid: unified codebase, detailed hyperparameter tables, hardware specification, and a promise of code release.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: ADMM for pruning/quantization is well established (e.g., Huang et al. 2021 cited by the authors), and the components (Adam second-moment Fisher approximation, magnitude-based projection, quantized states) are largely assembled from existing techniques; the contribution is primarily a careful application at scale rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Some recent competitive baselines are cited but not empirically compared, e.g., MaskLLM (Fang et al., 2024) and ProxSparse (Liu et al., 2025), both of which target high-sparsity LLM pruning; the comparison space could also include iterative/fine-tuning-based global pruning beyond the Wanda+LoRA/Full retraining baselines.

ELSA is not uniformly better: at moderate sparsity (50-60%), it is often behind SAFE/ALPS in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy (Tables 10-12), and it is not the best method under N:M 2:4/4:8 patterns (Table 8). The advantage is confined to the high-sparsity regime; the paper should state this more explicitly rather than only in passing.

The 'surrogate-free' framing is somewhat overstated: ELSA still optimizes on a finite 32,768-sequence calibration/training set from C4 (evaluated also on C4), so it approximates the true objective rather than solving it; the risk of overfitting to calibration data and train/evaluation dataset overlap deserves more analysis.

Theoretical assumptions are strong relative to the actual setting (weak convexity, bounded iterates, exactness conditions on λ and γ) and the result is a standard λ-stationarity guarantee; the theory supports plausibility rather than explaining why the method works so well empirically.

Minor presentation issues: several typos (e.g., 'researchers has begun', 'constrat'), incomplete sentence in B.1 (dangling link), and the Fisher-diagonal approximation is justified somewhat briefly; also unstructured sparsity speedup depends on the specific MACKO kernel, so generality of the acceleration claims is limited to that ecosystem.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six architectures/scales (125M–27B), eight baselines, perplexity and zero-shot benchmarks, plus N:M and non-uniform sparsity extensions

Demonstrates convincing gains in the high-sparsity regime (80–95%) where competing methods collapse, with a Pareto analysis (Fig. 3), extreme-sparsity study up to 99%, and end-to-end latency/throughput/memory benchmarks using a real SpMV kernel
Honest cost analysis (Table 3) quantifying the pruning compute of ELSA versus one-shot and retraining baselines, which strengthens the practical claims
Useful ablations (NTP vs. reconstruction objective under varying data; objective-aware Fisher-diagonal projection) that support the paper's central design choices
Convergence analysis provided for both ELSA and the quantized ELSA-L variant, adding theoretical grounding beyond heuristics
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: ADMM-based pruning with L0 constraints is a well-established technique (e.g., Huang et al. 2021, which the paper itself cites, and older ADMM pruning work); the contribution is essentially a globalization of layer-wise ADMM (Boža 2024) plus a diagonal-Fisher projection and quantized states — an engineering combination rather than a fundamentally new method

The 'surrogate-free' framing overstates the contrast: ELSA is effectively a retraining method (32,768 datapoints, ~1024 steps, multi-GPU), making it not directly comparable to one-shot pruners like Wanda/SparseGPT; although the cost analysis helps, the headline comparison '7.8x less perplexity than the best existing method' mixes methods with very different compute budgets

At moderate sparsity (50–60%), ELSA is consistently worse than baselines (e.g., LLaMA-2-7B 50%: 7.5/9.81 vs. SAFE 6.72/8.87; OPT-125M 50%: 37.68 vs. ALPS 32.70), so the method only shines in the regime where all others fail — the value of a method that requires full retraining-style compute to reach 80–90% sparsity versus simply retraining strong one-shot pruners is only partially addressed

Claims of 'retaining high model fidelity' and 'without significant performance degradation' are overstated: at 90% sparsity, zero-shot average accuracy (38.52) is far below dense (59.67), and perplexity roughly doubles relative to dense; the achieved quality may not be genuinely 'usable' in practice

Theoretical contribution is modest and its assumptions are strong/idealized: exact or near-exact x-update stationarity (Algorithm 1 assumes the quantized dual update error vanishes in the limit), bounded iterates, weak convexity; the resulting λ-stationarity guarantee is a weak notion and the gap between theory and the practical inexact implementation is not discussed

Per-model, per-sparsity hyperparameter tuning (Tables 4–6, with many empty/incomplete cells) raises questions about robustness and reproducibility; the prose also contains missing URLs and numerous typographical errors, suggesting a rushed manuscript
Zero-shot evaluation is limited to LLaMA-2-7B/13B; other models are evaluated only by perplexity, and some radar plots/figures are difficult to parse quantitatively

strengths: The paper challenges the widely held 'sparsity wall' narrative in LLM pruning and provides a principled diagnosis: the layer-wise reconstruction surrogate objective, its error compounding, and restricted search space. This framing is well-argued and supported by citations.

The method is technically sound: reformulating pruning as a sparsity-constrained problem and solving it with ADMM, including an objective-aware (Fisher/diagonal-Hessian) projection step that reuses Adam second-moment estimates at negligible cost, is elegant and well-motivated.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: four architectures (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2/3) across scales from 125M to 27B, perplexity and seven zero-shot tasks, comparisons against eight baselines including recent strong ones (ALPS, L-ADMM, SAFE, SparseLLM).

Practical relevance is demonstrated beyond perplexity: end-to-end latency/throughput/memory measurements with an actual SpMV kernel (MACKO), a cost-quality analysis (GPU-hours vs. perplexity), and a memory-efficient variant (ELSA-L) that scales to 27B models.

The paper includes convergence guarantees for both ELSA and the quantized ELSA-L variant, plus useful ablations (NTP vs. REM objective, geometric projection, non-uniform and N:M sparsity patterns), and reasonable reproducibility details (hyperparameter tables, hardware configurations).
weaknesses: ELSA does not consistently win in the moderate-sparsity regime (50-60%): in Tables 10-12 it frequently trails L-ADMM/ALPS/SAFE at these levels (e.g., OPT-125M 50% and LLaMA-2-7B 50% zero-shot). The contribution is effectively restricted to high-sparsity regimes, and the paper should frame claims accordingly rather than as a general advance.

Absolute performance at extreme sparsity is still far from dense: at 90% sparsity on LLaMA-2-7B, perplexity is 26.97 vs. 5.47 dense (roughly 5x) and average zero-shot accuracy drops from 59.67 to 38.52. Phrases like 'retaining high model fidelity' and 'without significant performance degradation' overstate the evidence.

Fairness of comparison is a concern: ELSA is a full fine-tuning-based iterative method using 32,768 datapoints vs. 128 calibration sequences for one-shot baselines. The cost analysis (Table 3) is appreciated and partially addresses this, but stronger retraining-based baselines (e.g., iterative magnitude pruning with retraining, or mask-search plus fine-tuning at matched compute) are missing; Wanda+Full/LoRA is only a partial attempt.

The convergence theory has notable caveats: it relies on strong assumptions (bounded iterates, weak convexity), the x-update is only approximately solved within a gamma-ball, lambda-stationarity is a weak notion, and the diagonal Fisher approximation used in practice diverges from the analyzed algorithm. The theory is more of a sanity check than a guarantee for the deployed method.
Some claims in the discussion (e.g., that layer-wise methods' memory advantage is 'somewhat inflated' via offloading) are speculative and not backed by experiments.

Code is only promised ('will be made available'), not yet released, which weakens reproducibility at review time; a few cited recent methods (e.g., ProxSparse, MaskLLM) are not included in comparisons.
